paragraphs.text: The story of the life of the holy Peter the Iberian, bishop and confessor, the chosen and humble servant of our Lord.

…that we should remember our leaders. We have been commanded to do so by Paul, the divine apostle, who says: "Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their conduct and imitate their faith." So, as people who are paying a fitting debt that is pleasing to God, and fulfilling the apostolic command, we are eager to do this. For it is truly a great way of salvation for disciples who are zealous for what is good, and eager to be made like them, to follow the excellent conduct of those who were leaders in God. But the memory set before us is not only that of a leader. It is that of a good shepherd, a father who loved us, a holy bishop, a confessor of the fear of God, and a martyr many times over: one who is loved by all alike, both by the one who speaks and by those who listen. So it is right that we should speak and hear about him with all eagerness, trusting in his holy prayers. And even if we cannot pay the debt as it deserves, yet

with goodwill we may pay it as far as we are able. We make the beginning of our account of him the origin and birth of his family, because of what is fittingly said: "God is with the generation of the righteous," and "The generation of the upright shall be blessed," and "a chosen race and a royal priesthood." The homeland of the blessed Peter, then, was the country of the Iberians, famous among those northern peoples who are situated toward the East. It is constantly fought over by the Romans and the Persians, each of them eager to make the country its own through friendship and alliance. In the language of their country he was first called Nabarnugios. But when he was deemed worthy of the holy monastic habit, his name was changed to Peter, after the chief of the apostles. The fathers who gave him the holy habit were moved, I think, by divine inspiration, because he was going to be zealous in his conduct, in his ways, and in the boldness of the faith entrusted to him by God. It was for the sake of this faith that our Lord named the apostle Peter, that is, Kepha, "rock," and founded the orthodox church upon this rock, saying to him: "You are the rock, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Sheol shall not overcome it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be

loosed in heaven." The father of our blessed father and bishop Peter was Bosmarios, king of the Iberians. His father's father was Bosmarios. His mother was Bakurduktia, and his mother's mother was the holy Duktia. His maternal grandfather was the great Bakurios, the husband of Duktia. Bakurios was the first of those who reigned in that country to become a Christian king, and he guided that whole people to the fear of God. Though they were all kings and queens of the Iberians, through virtue they also gained the kingdom of heaven. His paternal grandmother was Osduktia, the wife of Bosmarios and the mother of his father Bosmarios. Pharasmanes was the brother of Osduktia, his paternal grandmother. He held a distinguished place at the court of Arcadius, king of the Romans, with the rank of commander-in-chief, and he held the foremost positions. In the end he fled the schemes of Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, and managed to hide, and with difficulty he reached his own country. When he became king over the Iberians, he took the Huns with him as allies. These are neighbours of the Iberians, and they have caused many evils for those who are subject to the Romans. The great Bakurios, the maternal grandfather of the blessed Peter, had a brother, the holy Arsilios. He grew old together with Bakurios and Bosmarios, from the time of the Iberians' rule,

and he completed his life in virginity and in all holiness. The blessed Peter had no full brothers or sisters. He had only a half-sister on his father's side, born of a concubine, whose name was Bumirosparia. By his father's wish she was counted as a full sister. A holy and renowned woman named Zuzo brought up Peter while he was still a child. He was hidden in her house so that he would not be handed over to the Persians as a hostage, for they had sent envoys about this many times. Her daughter, who was called Oṭa, was the blessed one's nurse, and she also suckled him when he was an infant. Her husband was Kurianios, and her full brother was Bardelios. Their sons, Qaṭa and Morgaqis, were the blessed one's foster brothers and companions of his own age. Let no one with a narrow mind think this list of names superfluous. We have not mentioned them for nothing. That father, who loved love and truly loved God, used to gather all these names together on one day each year, the Saturday of the middle week of the Fast, and celebrate their commemoration. He did this to repay them for the quiet life they had granted him, the life he had chosen for himself when he stripped off the world. Therefore we too, though lesser men, have thought it right not to neglect the memory of those he thought worthy of remembrance, from whom such a flower blossomed. For there may be some, even among the nobility, who will grow in love of virtue when they hear the story of these people. The great Bakurios,

who was the first of the kings of the Iberians to become a Christian, and Duktia his consort reached such heights of the fear of God, of the virtues, and of life in Christ that, even while they were kings and reigned, they practised and lived the monastic life. With one accord and in good harmony they agreed to abstain from bodily union, content with the children who had already been given to them. The faithful Bakurios gave himself to fasting, prayer and almsgiving. Three times a week he swept the city's church with his own hands. He abounded in love for the poor, and he never failed to have various dishes prepared in his palace. He would carry them in baskets by night to the poorhouse he had built, and there the king fed those who lay sick with his own hands. The blessed Duktia, his consort and partner in zeal, cast off all her royal adornment and clothed herself in sackcloth. She sold all the gold and pearls of her litter, the kind called a basterna, and distributed the money to the poor. Often she spent whole weeks in fasting and prayer, and she received from our Lord such grace that she had only to lay her hands on the sick and they were healed. As for the great Bakurios, her husband,

this story must not be passed over. Along with his other virtues, he once also wove the crown of confession, and indeed, in intention, that of martyrdom as well. He once went to war with the king of the Persians, since he had made a treaty of peace with him, and he went as his commander-in-chief. At sunrise he saw the king and all the generals and high officers, the satraps and all the nobles, immediately dismount from their horses and worship the sun, while he remained sitting on his horse. Other satraps reported this to the king. When Bakurios stood before him and was asked whether what had been said about him was true, he cried out boldly before the whole army, a true rival in zeal of Daniel and of the three youths, his companions: "I am a Christian, and it is not permitted for me to abandon him who alone is the true God and Creator of all, and to worship his creation, which was made to give light for my service and for the service of all mankind." The king was greatly amazed and abashed by his boldness. He turned and said privately to his own men, "He is Bakurios, and we need him. What can we do to him?" These are some of the victories of Bakurios. His full brother Arsilios, whom we mentioned above, lived in old age and in virginity as a son of the royal house of the Iberians, together with Bosmarios, the father

of our Peter, who was also called Nabarnugios. The leading men of the country pressed and implored him earnestly to marry, so that children might be born and the royal succession continued. They brought him a wife of royal family, but he remained a virgin with her. Then he learned that she had done something shameful. She denied it, though he rebuked her gently. In the end he summoned that wicked man at once, and (oh, the humility and great gentleness of his philosophy!) said to him: "Look, I grant you your life and your blood. Here are provisions and money for the journey. Leave quickly, and do not stay in this country, or you may die a terrible death and your blood be counted against me." When he had sent him away like this, he said to his wife: "Because you have done this, I will not let you go, nor will I expose your shame. But I trust in the Son of God, whose law you have wronged, that he will make worms spring from your loins, and so your flesh will be consumed." Immediately the curse of that chaste man took effect. The part of her body below the belly rotted with worms, and her life and flesh were bitterly consumed, so that she went about as nothing but dry bones and skin. Yet the zeal of that righteous man also brought forth salvation from the curse. Chastened by the stroke from God, she came to confess the truth and was filled with deep repentance. She groaned bitterly

as she turned to confession and repentance, and contrition of heart overwhelmed her completely. She threw herself down in public before the door of the church, confessed her sin before everyone, and begged them all to trample on her, calling herself an adulteress, a disgraced and unfaithful woman, an enemy of God and a reproach to mankind. So she moved everyone to pity, tears and compassion. The whole people fasted together, and the church prayed earnestly and constantly for her with tears and groans, and she was healed of the stroke. After this the holy woman lived in such excellence and humility that she became a model and example to everyone of the way of grace and salvation. Through his excellent conduct, this faithful Arsilios found such grace and boldness before God that he worked miracles through his prayers. So our blessed father used to affirm, testifying to nothing false. While he was reigning over the Iberians, he learned that the blessed Peter had left the world, was living in the holy city, and was practising the monastic life there. So, as the matter was guided by God who reveals it, he sent word to him, saying: "Since it is written, 'Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and members of his household in Jerusalem,' as we have you, I beg you, my son, to pray for me, so that through

your prayers I may find mercy." Many of the great men of the earth, lovers of pleasure (even believers among them), have a custom of keeping male and female singers, those vanities of the world, who sing for entertainment and corrupting pleasure. He instead appointed singers of priestly songs, like King David, who sang the holy words of God at meals and at all hours, so that his palace would differ in no way from a church. Osduktia, the paternal grandmother of the blessed Peter, was so holy that after her death, when a building of some kind, a shrine, was being put up and kept collapsing in earthquakes, they brought her body and placed it there as one of the saints, and at once the collapses stopped. The blessed Zuzo, who brought up the blessed one, was so holy that when he was a little child sleeping at her side, she often drenched him with tears as she stood at night, saying in the Iberian language: "My Lord Jesus, my God, the giver of my life, have mercy on me." Once there was an earthquake and everything shook. The blessed woman ran around her house, which had eight conches [?], clasped each of the pillars and cried out boldly: "Lord, see how I have served you, and spare me and my children." Her prayer did not allow her house to suffer any damage, even though the earthquake then overturned a great many houses. There was

in that city a certain man, one of the notables, who was greedy and wronged many people. Though she rebuked him many times, he did not give up his greed. Then she prayed, and at once fire came down from heaven and consumed all his fields, which were then close to harvest. Her daughter, called Oṭa, who was also the blessed one's nurse, spent all her days in holiness, fasting and prayer. The mother of our holy father, Bakurduktia, remained a widow after her husband's death. She was not drawn to become the wife of a second husband, but persevered in fasting and prayer. She would no longer live in the city. Instead she chose to live the monastic life on her estates, and everywhere she built guesthouses for strangers and houses for the sick. When the blessed one heard that she was going to come and visit him, he fled to Cyprus so as not to see her face. When she learned this, she did not come again. Indeed, from the time he took the monastic habit, he never once wished to write to any of his family or to receive letters from anyone. He told us this himself many times. From such a holy root and such holy forefathers the rose blossomed, the blessed and holy Peter, and he was raised by such God-fearing foster parents. Rightly, and in a way worthy of those who bore him and brought him up, he became a chosen vessel, as it is written, "honoured, sanctified and useful to his Master, and prepared for every good work," to bear the name of Christ and to praise and proclaim the orthodox faith before all people, from his childhood until his last breath. He remained a disciple

of the apostles and their exact imitator, always carrying the cross of Christ and full of the Holy Spirit. Through his grace and power he drew many to obey Christ and the Gospel. He offered himself as a model of everything good and of excellent conduct, in keeping with the apostle's admonition, "in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity." He was a glorious pillar of the orthodox faith, and by his holy prayers a wall for the whole world, like Noah long ago when the ark was tossed in the final flood of rebellion. But his manifold virtues in God, and his evangelical conduct, which showed themselves above all at every stage of his life and grew with him by divine grace, are not something that the weakness and poverty of our words should attempt to describe worthily or bring to completion. For I fear that I may find myself walking into a boundless, unfathomable abyss of his achievements, and since I can swim neither with experience nor with skill, I may be swept away and drowned by the floods of the waves of grace that surrounded him. Because of my lowliness and weakness, let his excellence bear with what is lacking. From here, then, each of his ways of life and his successes, which were displayed by the grace of God at various times, in various ways and in various deeds, in humility and asceticism, and, as the apostle says, "in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses, in persecutions, in labours, in fasts, in vigils, in beatings," in struggles and in contests to the point of blood, not only against sin, nor against blood and flesh, but against principalities and authorities,

against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the spirits of wickedness; in great endurance, in the power of signs, wonders and healings, in the power of the Holy Spirit, with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, in glory and in dishonour, in blasphemies and in praises. He was as one unknown, yet known; and he was known to his God alone, as far as it was right for him to be known. He was as one dead to the flesh, yet always alive and fervent in spirit; as poor, yet making many rich, feeding souls and bodies with the food that suited each; as having nothing, yet possessing everything, not only on earth but in the treasuries of heaven. For there he had treasures laid up, where his heart, his mind and his conduct always were. All these things, and everything connected with them, were accomplished excellently by him for the zeal and salvation of many, through the grace of Christ who dwelt in him. Since I cannot make them known accurately and truthfully, or write them out in a narrative, I leave them aside. I refer those who love such things to the mouths of all those saints of former days who heard them many times, things that are written as though in priestly books. I advise such a reader to seek them out and be filled with knowledge and profit from them. For they are well known everywhere, and even if no one asks, they are proclaimed by divine grace. Let no one disbelieve what is told, but let him consider that what he hears falls short of the truth. For what time or what words would be enough to tell

accurately what the grace of Christ accomplished through his hands and with him, for the salvation, as I said, and the healing of those who wished to be zealous for good things? Then there is the confirmation, the building up and the strengthening of many in the orthodox faith and in its catholic church, in which the High Priest and Shepherd appointed him. And how did this happen? Let no one say, like those who love to find fault, that he took and seized such an honour for himself. Rather, he was called by grace from above, with a calling that was in some way divine and worthy of wonder. Even in haste I cannot pass over it. Instead I will make it known as best I can, briefly, taking my account back a little to its beginning. Like the patriarch Isaac, he too was conceived and born in fulfilment of a promise. Let the manner of it be told now, at the right moment and briefly. His father Bosmarios was returning from an estate outside the city to come into the city, and he reached a river on the way. It was in full flood, and the crossing on the road was blocked. He was forced to spend the night on its bank. While he was deep in thought [?], he saw a man who said to him: "Bosmarios, look, the river has become passable for you. Get up, cross over and go into your house. Lie with your wife, and she will conceive and bear you a son, who will be honoured before God and before men." So by such divine grace he was conceived, born and brought up. When he was still only twelve years old, he was sent as a hostage

to the God-fearing and Christian Theodosius the Younger, king of the Romans. Theodosius had pressed for this many times, sending envoys, and so the boy was sent by his father Bosmarios, who reigned over the land of the Iberians at that time and valued the friendship of the Romans, as Christians, above the help of the wicked Persians. He was sent with great pomp and honour. When he came to the blessed Theodosius, he was received warmly, and was brought up and loved by him as a son. He saw the zeal for the fear of God and the love of Christ shown by the king, by Queen Eudocia, his consort and partner in zeal, by the men and women who served them, and especially by the eunuchs called cubicularii. All of them lived in the palace as though in a monastery, with prayers, fasts, night vigils, and the other things that please God. Seeing this, he was set on fire with zeal. He already had from his forefathers at home the love of God, like a spark of fire. Through ascetic exertions and humility he fanned it day by day with increasing zeal, until he made it into a great flame, a blazing coal of heavenly grace for his soul. Underneath, against his body, he wore a garment of hair, while outside he wrapped himself in a splendid and magnificent robe to hide his virtue. His food was what Daniel and his companions ate, and only a small measure of it. He took it once every three days

or every four, and sometimes only once a week, as one who loved discipline for subduing the flesh and the unruly impulses of youth. His bed was the ground, though he was a king, a child, and delicate. As he governed himself in this way, cleansing himself of every defilement of flesh and spirit and growing in years, he became a temple of God, filled with the Holy Spirit. All this happened so that by divine grace, while he was still a child, many healings, signs and great miracles were accomplished by his hands in that very palace. Since I do not want to weary my hearers altogether, I will leave the others aside and first set down one of them, which is enough to confirm them all. He had the bones of holy martyrs who were Persians by birth and had recently been martyred in those times. Following the blessed one's tradition and custom, we still honour their names, celebrate their commemorations and read the accounts of their martyrdom. He had placed them with honour in a reliquary [?] in the very bedchamber where he practised his asceticism. There he slept before them on the ground, and performed divine services with lamps, incense, hymns and supplications. And as he offered them every honour and refreshment, he saw

them openly many times, singing with him, keeping vigil with him and praying with him. Once, when the holy feast of Epiphany came, on which all the senators are required to celebrate the feast, see the king and be seen by one another, he shut himself in the martyrs' bedchamber. With his own hands he did all the decorating of that house of prayer, cleaning the walls [?] and the ceiling, and sweeping and washing the floor. Then he washed many lamps, polished them with a cloth, and hung them all around. He sent to his steward and ordered him to bring oil to light the lamps. But the steward was steeped in the follies of the world, and wanted to see him behave like the other nobles of the court; or rather, he was being used by the Devil. He turned angry and said: "Fine hopes indeed, for him, for his country and for us! He was sent by them to the Romans for honour and royal glory, and he wants to become a monk and make wretches of all of us who are attached to him!" And he would not send oil. But the holy child, a philosopher, recognised the work of the Adversary. At such a young age he showed evangelical exactness with meekness and patience of spirit, and turned his anger into prayer. Fervent in faith and spirit, he called upon the prayers of those saints, and when the hour of his evening vigil arrived, using water

alone, without oil, he prepared and lit all the lamps. Throughout the seven days of the holy feast they went on burning, night and day, without ceasing. When the king, all his household and the senate heard of this, they were all amazed. Many came to long to emulate his conduct and his humility, and a considerable number of such people, who practised asceticism with him and were found worthy to share his zeal, gathered around him. So one day, as he stood among them and talked with them about their salvation, he suddenly saw our Lord among them in the dress of an ascetic. He fell down and worshipped him at his feet. No one saw him except Peter alone, and he cried out with weeping and tears, "My Lord and my God!" He thought the others could see him too, but they did not; he alone saw. Then all those with him were filled with great amazement, fear and trembling, and when they understood the divine vision that had appeared to him, their divine zeal and love grew even greater. For this reason most of them renounced the world and took the habit after he became a monk. He used to tell us their names as well. Among them was the God-clothed monk Theodotus and his brothers Proclus and Sophronius, men renowned in authority. They were sons

and stewards of the imperial estate. But these are only a very few of the many achievements of the blessed one while he was a child, living as a sojourner in the palace. As he advanced in age and in divine love, he set ascents in his heart, as David, the singer of priestly songs, says, and passed from light to light, ever higher and clearer. He longed to depart from the world and its vanity and to hasten toward the first of the virtues, which is exile from one's homeland. Many times he tried to flee but could not, because the Devil and the demons kept betraying his plans. And the men of his household (his slaves, I mean, the spear-bearers who escorted him) were driven by their hatred of him to such anger that many times they tried to kill him secretly. Had the protection of the Lord alone not prevented it, they would have carried out their insolent plans. Nor were they the only ones. The God-fearing King Theodosius too was anxious to keep him as a hostage. He feared that if that people demanded him back and he could not produce him as he had received him, he would turn friends and helpers into enemies and fighters. So he summoned him and threatened him about this, and kept him under close guard so that he could not flee secretly. But there is nothing

stronger than the power of Christ, nor warmer than the love of those who love him purely. Christ loved him from childhood, as he loved Samuel. He shepherded him as he did Israel, and like Joseph, so also he guided and protected him like a lamb. He brought to fulfilment his good desire for the monastic habit with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, through signs and wonders, as he once snatched Israel from the tyranny of the Egyptians and brought them into the promised land, which flows with milk and honey. As helpers in his flight, as guides, guards and escorts, he appointed for him the holy martyrs, whom Peter had so honoured and given rest. For the more the love of flight from the world burned in him, the more the demons, and the men who were their helpers, hindered him, watching vigilantly and carefully over his coming in and going out, his wishes and his thoughts. Then he found the one given to him by God, the blessed John the eunuch [marginal note], who shared his ways and his zeal, was worthy with him of the longing for eternal life, and was a helper on the road that leads there. John was by birth from the land of the Lazi, and was adorned with every kind of fear of God, modesty, chastity, faith and humility. Peter took him as his companion, united him to himself and bound him in the bond of love, as Paul did

Barnabas, and he made him his counsellor and his companion in the flight of salvation. He knew that it is the work of the demons that people's thoughts are not hidden but are found out and exposed by them. So he took John close to the reliquary where the bones of the holy martyrs were laid. They both put their heads over the bones, and there they spoke with each other and made an agreement about the time and manner of their flight. From then on no one knew of it or revealed it, neither demons nor men, until the plan was carried out. They took the holy martyrs with them by night, without anyone knowing, past so many guard posts, in a royal city of such size and character. The martyrs also filled their hearts with great courage and strength. For they appeared to them, as I often heard when the blessed one told those who loved him (people who could profit from such stories), like a cloud or a pillar of fire, going before them in the darkness to lead and guide them. Or, wonderful to tell, they praised and sang in perfect harmony, with a melodious and sweet voice, this divine hymn, whose words I also set down. They are these: "Seek Christ, and see light from light and glory unspeakable; and for those who seek it, this becomes the payment of their reward." The blessed one also remembered the very melody of the hymn

And they did not stop singing openly in this way, while the holy martyrs went on ahead of them and guided them, until they reached the harbour. When they knew that they were now safe, they confidently looked for a ship. And when, by the help and assistance of the martyrs, they found one, they crossed over at once. But they were afraid that they might be caught, either by those pursuing them or by being recognised at the place called Stenon, for after their departure the gates and harbours of the city were watched, so that they were searched for over three days. So they put on another kind of dress, poor and fit for slaves. Through the protection of God, who went with them and guided them, they managed not to be recognised by those who were sitting at the Stenon and watching for them. From there they left the ship and went on foot. Through the region of Hyperos [?] the two of them made their journey alone, with the holy martyrs who were their guardians and companions, carrying their precious bones in a small golden casket, as the great Moses carried the ark of God with the cherubim. The only other thing they carried was a small book of John the Evangelist, in which was set a portion of the wood of the holy, precious and saving Cross. By it they were kept safe, and through it our Lord showed many signs and wonders of no small power, as He gave a gentle working through it to strengthen and comfort them. For it continued

for the whole week of their journey, that portion of the Cross pouring out oil in abundance, so much that they caught it in their hands and anointed their faces and their bodies, and still the oil flowed out more abundantly. And perhaps this is what the prophet calls “the oil of gladness”: the grace and power of the Holy Spirit, which rejoiced and exulted together with the power of the Cross that those holy ones had set out to take up, so as to follow with zeal the God who was crucified. It increased their zeal all the more and confirmed it through such wonders. This same grace also announced their coming through the holy martyrs. For as they travelled along the road and passed through regions, cities and villages, though they were entirely unknown both to the inhabitants of those regions and to those travelling with them, in most places they would find, outside the gates and outside the inns, crowds of children, men and women with branches and torches, as though they had come out to meet martyrs, sitting outside the walls. And they would ask those who arrived where they were and who they were, the people carrying the bones of the holy martyrs. For they said that on the day before, some men had come to them, announcing and instructing them to go out and meet them. So, greatly amazed at our Lord's care for them, their zeal and firmness of heart increased still more, so that they travelled lightly and without toil, with courage

and joy, as people shielded by such a hand. Now a certain man of those called bar adrē [?], a man of known authority, overtook them on the road and supposed that they were runaway slaves. Expecting to take them for his own service and slavery, he shook their minds with fear and threats and ordered them to go with him. And they followed him. For what else could they do, being like foreign slaves and captives being led away, except lift their eyes up to the Lord, and cry out in their hearts and call upon their guardians, the holy martyrs? That very night these came upon the man with many scourges, threatening utter destruction to him and to his whole house unless he released the young men in peace, as men of God who took refuge in them and trusted in them. And they warned him to release them with honour. So, in fear and trembling, he came at once at dawn and fell on his face before them, pleading with them [?]. He urged them strongly to stay in his district, promising to build them a monastery, to assign it sufficient revenue, and to provide them with every comfort, for the man was wealthy in that region. When they were not persuaded, he released them with many honours and comforts, as masters and benefactors, he who had earlier thought he would be their master. Having thus been released with honour and in a wonderful way,

the love and affection they had toward our Lord grew all the more in them, and so did their faith in the holy martyrs; and on every road and in every place they took delight in such care, protection and guidance from God, so that the word of Moses fitted them: “Like an eagle that shelters its nest and cherishes its young, spreads its wings and takes them up, and carries them on the strength of its pinions, the Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them. He surrounded them and guided them, and guarded them like the apple of the eye. He provided for them on the way; He brought them up and settled them on the heights of the holy land.” Rejoicing and exulting together, they made the journey from New Rome to Jerusalem as though it were a short road, passing continually from one stranger to another and from people unknown to people unknown, and through the love that was seething in them, which constantly stole away and soothed the weariness of the journey. When they were near Jerusalem, the holy city that was so beloved to them, they saw from a height that lies opposite it, about five stades away, the lofty roof of the holy and venerable churches gleaming like the dawning of the sun: that of the saving and venerable Cross, of the holy Resurrection, and also of the venerable Ascension on the mountain opposite it. And they cried out loudly, completing the prophetic word: “Behold Zion,

the city of our salvation! Your eyes shall see Jerusalem!” And they offered praise and thanksgiving, as far as their strength allowed, to Christ who loved them, who had called them, brought them out, guided them and saved them. Throwing themselves on their faces, they did not stop prostrating themselves from the top of that height, and they crept forward on their knees, all the while kissing that holy land with their lips and their eyes, out of the fullness of the love that was blazing in them, until they were within the holy walls. And they embraced the base of the precious Cross, I mean of holy Golgotha and the holy Resurrection, weeping together, giving thanks, praising and exulting, as though they had already received Jesus who loved them and were already with Him in heaven. And since I will cut the account short, leaving out many things: God, who had kept and saved them, since they were strangers and inexperienced in these holy places, guided them to good receivers of strangers, teachers and helpers of their holy desire, who were the first to show them good hospitality. I mean the blessed Melania the Roman, who, with Pinianus her husband and with Albina her mother, were foremost in the senate of Rome, and in lineage, wealth, glory and every kind of splendour, so that they even shared in royal descent. They loved Christ with a true love and honoured Him above everything

and laid up for themselves the wealth that endures and truly remains, in place of that which flows away, is dragged off, decays and corrupts. Despising all these things, they followed Him, having renounced the world completely. Most of what they had, whatever could easily be moved, they distributed to the poor and needy in every place under the dominion of the Romans, and they also gave it out among the holy churches and monasteries. Leaving all the rest and counting it as dung, and lovingly armed with the Cross of our Lord, they came to worship Him in the holy city. When they had come and had grown to love living there, they founded two large monasteries with many people on the holy Mount of Olives, beside the holy Ascension, one of men and the other of women. And they assigned revenue to both, for the glory and praise of God and for the reception and salvation of the many souls who come there for their salvation. Living in them in quietness, in all humility, stillness, abstinence and lowliness, they fought the good fight, humbling themselves even in their dress. For their clothing was of [?] coarse cloth, a lowly and despised garment. And keeping the new yoke of crucifixion with Christ, they were fed daily by the labour of their hands with what the weakness of the body required. Pinianus carried wood on his shoulders from the desert far away and sold it in the market without shame. And the blessed woman,

labouring at wool-work, supplied from it the small needs of her own sustenance and distributed the rest to the needy. So when she heard of the arrival in Jerusalem of Peter and John, the holy youths, who were then called Nabarnugius and Mithradates in the languages of their countries, and learned who they were and where they came from, she received them joyfully. For she remembered that once, when she had come to the royal city of Constantine, she had seen the blessed Peter there while he was still a boy being brought up at court. And she had loved him greatly, for she saw that the grace of Christ had been upon him from his childhood. For he was, as I have said, a lover of God from his youth. The reason the blessed Melania had come to the royal city was this. A man from among the nobles of Rome had come to the God-fearing emperor Theodosius, sent by the emperor Valentinian to betroth to him the daughter of the blessed Theodosius. This man was a kinsman of the holy Melania, but he did not yet share in the grace of the Christians. He wanted to see the blessed Melania, and he promised to become a Christian if he met her and heard from her the word of salvation. So, as I have said, the Christ-loving emperor sent and persuaded the blessed woman to come to the royal city

for the salvation of a soul. She came, and through the divine grace that dwelt in her she made him a believer and a perfect Christian. She edified many others and stirred them toward a divine way of life like her own, and she aroused still more the desire of the blessed Peter toward her zeal. Then she returned to the holy city, keeping to her former way of life and humility. Now since there was also another Melania in Jerusalem, one of the Roman nobility, who had likewise renounced the world and taken the habit, it is right to know that that one was the first, and this one, who received the saints, was the later. And before these two there was another woman, renowned in lineage and wealth, very chaste and God-fearing, whose name was Poemenia. She chose to live in the holy and venerable places, and by her way of life and her love those zealous women became renowned. She also built the church of the holy Ascension and adorned its buildings. And she overthrew the idol temple that stood on the mountain called Gerizim in Samaria, which was still standing and until that time was worshipped by the inhabitants of that region. This later Melania, then, the wife of Pinianus and daughter of Albina, is the one who received those holy ones with joy, as beloved sons. For when they had been received by her there, they were also honoured with the forms of the humble way of life in the monastery of the men. And together they were found worthy of the habit of the solitary life

from the holy hands of the holy and good Gerontius, who was priest and abbot of the monastery of the holy Mount of Olives. For this Gerontius, of whom it is good to speak, was a native of Jerusalem, and while still a child he had been taken into the service of a steward by the holy Melania and her husband. As he was brought up by them in holiness and in a way pleasing to God, it seemed fitting to them that he should share also in the priestly habit of the monastic life, as one who had a model to follow, and a way of life and conduct. So the two of them alone took him and brought him to the holy tomb of our Saviour, and laid the garments of the habit upon the holy rock, so that he might be clothed as if from the hands of our Lord. He asked that along with the priestly vesture he be granted these three things: orthodox faith, holiness and tears. And so he was found worthy of all three, and especially of the gift of tears. So when he was appointed both priest and abbot on the holy Mount of Olives and of the monasteries on it, many times on one day of the week he would celebrate three synaxes of the divine liturgy, especially on holy Sunday: one on the holy mount, one in the monastery of men, and another in the monastery of women. On the other days he would celebrate the synaxis and liturgy daily, privately, for the blessed Melania, according to the custom of the church of Rome. And at each of these synaxes, as soon as he began

the holy liturgy, he would shed tears without ceasing until the end, with pain and contrition of heart, so that none of those assembled could restrain himself; the whole congregation was moved to compunction, burning with weeping and sighs, and shedding tears like him. Rightly, then, having been found worthy of such a gift, he showed himself worthy of it even at the end. For when he reached the times of revolt, of the transgression of the Synod of Chalcedon, he showed a martyr's zeal in them, enduring bonds, prison and trials before judges, and he wove the crown of confession, and so he was perfected. And though he was strongly urged by rulers and by many distinguished persons merely to agree to speak with Juvenal the apostate, without communing with him, and so be freed from affliction, he refused altogether, saying, “The Lord forbid that I should see the face of Judas the traitor!” It was his hands that gave the habit to our fathers Peter and John. And he changed their names to these in place of the names they had been given in their countries. There they lived from then on in quietness and practised the excellence of humility, in the monastery of men, as I said before, of which this Gerontius was abbot. There too they then laid the precious bones of these holy martyrs, their good guides and companions, together with the bones of the forty good martyrs

of Sebaste, while Cyril, the holy and blessed archbishop of Alexandria, officiated at their deposition. For he had been urged by that faithful and glorious queen Eudocia to come for the deposition of the precious bones of Stephen, praised and excellent in all things, first of the martyrs and first of the deacons, and to perform the dedication of the beautiful church that she had built outside the northern gates of the holy city. He gladly accepted the invitation. He came with a large number of bishops from all Egypt and solemnly performed the deposition of the holy bones of the first of the martyrs on the fifteenth of the month of Iyyar. Then immediately afterwards, on the sixteenth of the same month, at the urging of the holy Melania, he also performed the deposition of the holy Persian martyrs, and of the forty martyrs with them, on the Mount of Olives, in a fine church that had likewise been splendidly built by Queen Eudocia herself, as the inscription written there on the wall makes known. But let us return to our subject. In this way, then, our father the champion was found worthy of the holy habit, when he had already passed twenty years of age, together with his fellow servant John. There he lived from then on in quietness and showed a way of life worthy of his habit, governing himself with abstinence and great humility; and the flesh, hard to bridle and prone to fall, which stands against

the spirit, whose will rebels against God in enmity and which cannot be subject to the law of God, he subdued and enslaved with hunger and thirst, with sleeping on the ground and with vigils, and with these harsh practices. All this he directed toward humility, until he had strangled the turbulence of the impulses of youth and quenched the flame of the passions. Then he readily allowed it to be subjected to the spirit, so that the spirit might be occupied with contemplation and rule over the flesh, and he brought the two together into a single gentle peace. Within dry skin and bones he confined that great strength and beauty of body, so that from then on he became bent, stooping from the great amount of mortification and from his great humility, he who had formerly been very robust and very imposing in the size of his body. How many wars, then, how many contests, how many trials did he endure, as he fought without ceasing against the Accuser and against his demons, the spirits of wickedness, by night and by day, not only in dreams and apparitions but, as the saying goes, hand to hand and face to face! He would constantly withdraw and go to the desert of John, the first Forerunner, who was the first head and teacher of this kind of evangelical way of life. I mean the desert that stretches beside the Jordan. There he would carry out his discipline, conversing alone with God alone, and waging the contest of virtue all the more

eagerly and valiantly. And of what help and comfort from God he was found worthy, neither can the weakness of our speech write it down nor can the measure of time contain it. Therefore, while I pass over many things, I think it necessary to set down one that is especially worthy of remembrance and of telling, which happened to him at the beginning, when he had taken the habit, as an indication of the things passed over and for the benefit of those who hear. He saw the blessed Passarion, a great lover of the poor and lover of strangers, who, along with the rest of his virtues and righteous deeds before God, built a poorhouse outside the eastern gates of the city for the comfort and relief of those whose bodies are wretchedly afflicted by infirmity, and who founded within the walls of holy Zion a large and beautiful monastery for the service and psalmody of those who constantly and without ceasing praise the Lord. And he longed to become an imitator of this good work himself. He resolved that with the Lord's help he would build a house and establish there a certain number of holy monks praising the Lord. But before he began the work he fell ill, falling into a severe sickness. And while he lay grievously ill, he saw the Accuser standing before him, openly laughing and mocking and saying, “Look, see what the one you love has done to you! See where He has put you, the one you followed and for whose sake you left everything! Now say a word to Him and be healed.” But he blew upon him and took courage,

as one who had many times experienced his wickedness, and said to him, “For the sake of my Jesus, tell me, you unclean and wicked dog, who quarrel with God, you blasphemer: are you advising me to do your work? May the power of Christ destroy you!” And as soon as he heard the name of Christ, the evil one vanished like smoke and could no longer be seen. Then Peter began to weep, and with bitter tears and sighs to call upon the Lord. And at once the Lord appeared to him, as it is written: “While you are still speaking, He will say, ‘Here I am, I am near,’” and said to him, “What is the matter with you? Why are you troubled, you faint-hearted one? Do you not know that I have authority over life and death, and that it lies in my hands whether you live or die? But if you are grieved because you have not been allowed to fulfil the vow and promise you made, to build me a church as you first desired, lift up your eyes and see.” And when he looked up, as though toward heaven, he saw a church, beautiful and glorious, full of light and glory, and in it, standing in order and not in scattered groups, plainly visible, men ministering and singing, about fifty in number. And a voice came to him, saying, “Behold the church that you promised to build for me. Behold also those who sing! From now on do not be grieved.” When He had said these things, the Lord departed from him. And he worshipped and was filled with joy, and was filled all the more with strength, zeal and faith. And because he had been fully assured by this vision,

this is how the brothers who were with him came to stand and sing, arranging themselves in ordered ranks. And through his prayers this order has continued to this day and has been kept by his brothers. But let us return to the rest of the necessary narrative. Having lingered, as far as was possible, on a few small matters, let us take up again from where we left the account. For we remember that we promised to show, with God's help, how he moved from Jerusalem and came to live in the region of Gaza, a city by the sea, so that he was found worthy of the priesthood, and finally of the high priesthood, by the choice of divine grace.

Jerusalem, the holy city, the city of the great King, in which the saving mystery of the whole world was accomplished through the dawning of God and the salvation of Christ, had long ago been uprooted by the Romans after the audacity of the Jews against Christ, as all the prophets had foretold in their words and according to the decree of Christ's judgment. At last it was rebuilt anew and settled more spaciously in the times of Constantine, the Christ-loving and faithful emperor, the father and patriarch of all Christian kings, who was truly the chosen one, the new David; and through the fear of God of his mother, the blessed Helena, who was worthy of him in zeal and truly a new mother to him. For this queen, a lover of God, with warm faith, strengthened by the fear of God and by divine zeal,

and having her son as helper and partner in zeal, did not delay in coming herself to the holy places of Christ. First, having searched and found, with divine help, the saving wood of the precious Cross, she set it up for veneration and for the healing of souls and bodies for the whole world, for whose sake it had indeed been fixed. After that she raised for our Lord great and beautiful houses of God and beautiful churches over the divine tomb of our Lord and at the holy place of the Skull, venerable Golgotha, which is truly the holy of holies and the true altar. This altar was proclaimed in mystery long ago by the prophet Moses and prefigured as made of uncut and unworked stones, put together by nature. For what other altar is like this, but this altar alone, which is truly the altar of Christ, undivided, admitting neither cutting nor division, on which the true Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, was slain and offered? Now since the account has brought us to this point, and we have made mention of the venerable Cross, I think it right to set down in the narrative and bring before you a certain mystery and great and awesome wonder concerning its divine power, which took place in the presence of the blessed one, for the glory of God, for the full assurance of the hope of Christians, and for the support and confirmation of our faith. Of this the blessed one himself was witness and beholder,

our father, the son of a truly faithful woman, who himself also told of it many times and before many people, heeding the prophet who says, “Declare His greatness among the peoples, and tell of all His wonders, and glory in His holy name; remember His marvels that He has done.” For while he was still a boy, being brought up in the palace with the blessed emperor Theodosius, he managed to obtain a portion of the Cross from the clergy who, as was the custom, came from Jerusalem to honour the emperor and brought him blessings. He hid it in a small [?] cloth, which he wrapped around it with skilful work, and kept it carefully and reverently. He placed it in a golden case, and every week, and especially on the established feasts, he would bring it out, and after being blessed by it and kissing it, he would put it back in its place. Once, then, on one of those days, when he was doing this, having fallen on his face, kissed it and been blessed, he called one of the chamberlains who were with him, whom he regarded as more faithful and more intimate than the others, and who happened to be alone with him at the time, and urged him also to venerate it and be blessed. But when that man drew near and came to lay his face on that holy portion and be blessed, while it was still wrapped, as I said before, in the [?] cloth and its workmanship, it suddenly became a white dove. And flying from the hands of the saint, it circled around the house,

flying about and looking for a way out. When this happened, the blessed one was astonished and cried out. Leaping up, he went round and ran about the house, trying to catch the dove. But it found a way out through a window and vanished, and that portion was never seen again afterwards, together with the [?] cloth and its workmanship. The reason, as the blessed one came to understand through a vision, was that the young man was unworthy, for it so happened that he was not pure from defilements. Similar to this, the blessed one also told of another wonder, concerning the power of holy Golgotha and the divine grace hidden in it. Once a severe ringworm broke out on the face of the blessed John the eunuch and spread over his whole face, and both of them were distressed. It caused them great pain, and the blessed John was ashamed even to be seen by people. As their grief grew heavy and was consuming their hearts, the faithful Peter came to himself and, burning in spirit with divine fervour, took the blessed John by night, and the two of them went to the holy Resurrection. They went up to the place of holy Golgotha from the north side, since that spot was quiet and secluded, and knelt down, entreating our Lord with bitter tears and sighs. And when they had finished the prayer, and had risen and come forward to venerate the venerable rock of holy Golgotha, the blessed John saw

what looked like a hand, which came out from there, drew near to his face and wiped his whole face. And when morning came he was found to be completely clean, with no trace or mark of that sore remaining. These things are for the demonstration of the divine power of the holy Cross and for the full assurance of our hope. In the same way, I think it fitting to add to this narrative another wonder that happened at another time to the blessed John, to show their love for each other, their faith toward God and their boldness before Him. Once the blessed John fell into such a severe illness that he was despaired of, and father Peter was deeply broken and entreated the Lord without ceasing for his recovery. A voice came to him, saying, “Take courage. See, I am granting him recovery because of your request, and I am adding twelve more years to his life.” And so it came to pass. Then, wonderfully, as he recovered and began to regain strength, his body began to peel, shedding thick scales from his nails up to his neck. And all were anxious that the peeling, as it spread, might ruin his face as well; but when father Peter again entreated and prayed earnestly, it went no further than his neck. When he recovered, his body and his flesh became like those of a newborn child. But his voice became so unrecognisable that he could not say anything plainly and clearly. When one of the established feasts came round, however,

Father Peter urged him, as though by divine providence, to celebrate the holy offering for them. Both of them had been found worthy of the honour of the priesthood, and the blessed Peter also of the high priesthood. John kept excusing himself, saying that he could not speak and was unable. But Father Peter persisted, urging and pressing him. He said there was no need to shout, since one completes the prayers within the heart: “For even when we are silent, God hears.” When John was compelled, he gave in. He stood before the holy altar and said to the people, clearly and distinctly, “Peace be with you all,” and in this way he completed the whole holy offering. At once he received his former voice back from God, as if he had never been sick, and from then on he spoke well for the rest of his life. At this time the blessed John was in a vision for whole days. He spent three days in that vision and spoke with no one at all. He saw the fearful and glorious second coming of our Lord. The heavens were opened from above. He saw the trumpets sounding, the tremors of the world, the change or alteration of the elements, and all of it full of light, haste, pressure, commotion and tumult. He saw the angels running ahead, and the first ranks of the heavenly powers: angels, archangels, dominions, lordships and glories. He saw the ranks of the holy apostles, prophets, martyrs and righteous ones, the cherubim and the seraphim, and after all of them the worshipful sign

and the redeeming sign of the Lord’s cross. He saw the Lord himself, the Saviour and Christ, appearing and coming with the Father’s glory and ineffable power. He saw the thrones being prepared, and the divine and fearful court of judgement, which was foretold to us long ago and many times through the holy prophets, and by the Judge and Saviour himself, as a testimony. He also saw a single altar standing on the earth, like in every respect the one still kept among us today, at which the two of them were ministering. Around it stood a multitude of holy monks, each holding his staff. And behold, from above came the sounds of trumpets and the tumult of the elements, and something like flying clouds, which snatched up from that altar the saints standing around it to meet our Lord. He spent three days in such a vision and saw many other mysteries that no human being is permitted to tell. After this, when he came to himself, he remained in astonishment for about thirty days and did not wish to say anything to anyone. Nor indeed could he, for his mind was wholly there, and he no longer thought he was living on earth. His face became like the face of an angel, and his whole appearance was different from a human one. This vision, however, came later, after a long time. Since I have mentioned the altar, I will not conceal a sign that took place at it while it was being consecrated, as the blessed Peter many times

recounted to us. Later, in the times of the Chalcedonian apostasy, they moved and were living in Alexandria, and there they made this holy altar. While it was being consecrated, the blessed one plainly saw the holy Mark the Evangelist standing and consecrating it. Through his hands, by grace, miracles of this kind were performed, with many mighty works and healings, too many to be counted. We have neither the strength nor the time to tell them one by one. This vision, as I said, was revealed later, when they were living in Alexandria and being persecuted for the sake of orthodoxy. Now that we have finished the digression, we will return to the point where we left our narrative. We will recount the cause that brought them to that monastery between Gaza and Maiuma, where they were living when they were brought by force to the priesthood. The holy city of Jerusalem had been rebuilt anew by Constantine, the Christian emperor, but it was still small in population and had no wall at all, since the former wall had been demolished by the Romans. There were very few houses and inhabitants in it. The high priests and bishops who came afterwards in Jerusalem wanted a multitude of inhabitants to live in the city and a multitude of buildings to be built. So they gave authority to anyone who wished and was able to take, within that part of the city, any place

that pleased him, freely and without price, and to build a dwelling on it. So the blessed Peter too chose a place for himself up towards holy Zion, at what is called the Tower of David, and built a monastery there. It is still called today the monastery of the Iberians. It stands on the left as one comes to holy Zion, by the gate of the two [?] of the Tower. There he lived in quiet with John, his companion in solitude. I will not pass over a sign that happened there while they were building the place. It is this. A man of note among the clergy was their neighbour, and he too had taken a place and was building there. A dispute arose about the boundary, as happens among neighbours. John the Eunuch was outside with the workmen, and he appealed to that man gently and humbly, for this was his custom, since he resembled Moses in his meekness. But the man was insolent, and acted as though he had been grievously wronged because John had spoken against him at all. He struck the blessed one hard on the jaw, like the servant of Caiaphas. John swallowed the insult, though he was in great pain, and made no reply at all. He left the workmen and the man, who was full of rage, and went inside to Father Peter, holding his jaw in his hand and groaning, for the blow was painful. The two of them prayed and gave thanks to our Lord for the grace, because he had found them worthy to share in his blows. They said nothing to that man. The builders stopped

their work, and the two of them agreed to move and leave that place. At dawn the next day that wretched man was buried dead, though nothing had been wrong with him before. So it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem that God the Judge, who at all times was helping these saints, did not delay his anger at the insult done to them. The two of them now remained alone in that place. They still had money left over from what they had managed to take when they departed, although from that time on they had distributed a great deal everywhere to the holy monks and the poor. They decided to trade a good trade with what remained: to receive and refresh the strangers and poor who came from everywhere to worship at the holy places. Having laid in sufficient provisions, they received strangers in the manner of Abraham, both strangers and sojourners, and they never wearied of such services. It often happened that they had as many as ten tables in a single day, especially at the well-known feasts. Even so, they alone served everyone, while they themselves went out to spend the nights elsewhere [?]. The zeal of their souls overcame the weakness of nature, together with the love of Christ, by which they were strengthened. They were also comforted by a miracle. Once, when a crowd of strangers had gathered to them, they ran short of what was needed. As time was pressing, they were in distress, and they cried out secretly to God in their hearts, ashamed at the hardship the strangers were suffering. They went into the storeroom to see whether some leftover provisions had been overlooked and remained there,

and they found every vessel full of whatever it had held before. They spent a long time receiving strangers in this way. At last the holy Zeno, the solitary and prophet, gave them counsel. He was a disciple of the great Silvanus and was renowned everywhere. He advised them to enter a monastery again and to be trained further through submission and humility. He said to them: “Now that you have practised hospitality, come and take up the monastic life from now on, being disciplined in a monastery. This is of greater profit for those who are still young in years.” So they entered one of the holy monasteries, and conducted themselves with complete obedience, submission and abstinence. The Accuser could not bear the novelty of their humility. He set out to bring them down from their humility and their zeal, contriving all kinds of temptations for them. One day Father Peter was standing in the choir singing psalms with the brothers, and the Accuser showed him a naked and very beautiful woman. Peter alone saw the phantasm. He regarded the sight as defilement, so he covered his face and turned this way and that. The brothers were astonished and asked what the cause was. He cried out in a loud voice: “Lord Jesus, remove from before my eyes this shameful and filthy form and the loathsomeness of this phantasm, and leave me in peace.” As soon as the evil one heard the name of our Saviour, he immediately vanished. They spent some time in the monastery, as the holy Zeno had advised, and then, again through his foreknowledge, they returned

to their own monastery, and lived in quiet in the holy city. They no longer received strangers as before, for the money had run out, having been well administered. Instead they mortified themselves with great humility and harsh practices. But they were not allowed to live there for long. Eudocia the empress, wife of the believing emperor Theodosius the Younger, had taken up the zeal of Melania, whom we mentioned earlier. She too longed for quiet and for a life in the holy city, so that she might be near and worship in person at the saving sufferings that Christ, the King of glory, endured for us. She set out in royal fashion, made the journey through all the cities, came to the holy city she longed for, and was found worthy to worship there. When she learned that Father Peter was living there, she eagerly sought to see him, since he was her foster son and she had lovingly been like a mother to him in the palace. At first he asked to be left alone and not have to come out of his cell, because he considered it a temptation. But she persisted. She said that if he did not wish to come to her, she would certainly come to him, since she was about to cross from there to holy Zion anyway. He feared honours and the envy of men, so he came out once and spoke with her. She was edified by his great gentleness, his meekness, his modesty and also his wisdom, and he heard her say: “Blessed are you, my son, for you have chosen the good part.

Remember me in your holy prayers.” He answered her: “What boldness does a sinner have to pray?” She said to him: “Your sins be on my head, my son.” With that he returned to his cell and lived in quiet. When she persisted again and wanted to come to him, he immediately ran to the holy Zeno, the prophet mentioned earlier. As was his custom, he revealed his thoughts to him, for he always took counsel with him. He heard from him: “Save, save your soul!” Persuaded by this counsel, he left Jerusalem, the holy city. He left his monastery to men who had also renounced the world, and came and lived in the community that lies between Gaza and the small town called Maiuma. At that time it was full of many holy men, monks who carried their cross. His move to that place was arranged by divine care. For God, who is wise in all things and cares for our souls, was preparing in advance for that town, which lies on the seashore and is thoroughly Christian, a high priest and bishop worthy of it. This was especially needed in the time of the apostasy, when such a man was needed: a helper of godliness, a herald and guardian of the orthodox faith, and an envoy on behalf of our souls. He had great boldness before our Lord to make atonement for the sins of the people, as it is written, and he was able to sympathize with our weakness, since he was always praying for us. While, then,

he was living in this community, he went constantly with John, his cell-companion, to the holy Zeno, who at that time lived in the village of Kefar Se'arta, about fifteen miles from Gaza. He consulted him about all his thoughts, and walked ever more fervently on the straight path of excellence in God. Zeno loved him greatly, and Peter received from his grace. The blessed one used to recount: “Once when I came to him, the holy Zeno stood up to pray. He turned towards me and said to me, ‘Pray.’ I was silent, and he turned again and said to me, ‘Pray.’ This happened three times. I was astonished and trembled at it, and said to him, ‘Forgive me, my lord father. Do you not know that I am a layman and a sinner?’ He said, ‘Yes, yes, forgive me.’ Then he prayed and sat down.” Seven days later his ordination took place. It is right not to pass over in silence how it happened. While he was still living in the holy city, Juvenal, who was then bishop there, tried many times to ordain him but did not succeed, because God was hiding him. Once, when a synaxis was being held on holy Zion, Juvenal tried to send zealous men to seize him from his cell, which was near there. When they were about to come, an angel appeared to him and said: “Behold, they are coming to take you for ordination. Get up and flee from here.” Having escaped in this way, he guarded himself more carefully. When he was living in the territory of Maiuma, the bishop

of that place at the time was Paul, the nephew of Juvenal. He had sent to him [?]: when Peter first settled there, Paul had given the blessed Peter his word, at his request, that he would not lay a hand on him. Then a synod of many bishops was held at the commemoration of Victor, the martyr of glorious victory, and Paul revealed the secret to one of them and urged him to carry out the ordination. That bishop took with him as a helper the blessed Irenaeus, archimandrite of the monastery, who was a companion, neighbour and close friend of these saints. Through him he fell upon Peter suddenly and unexpectedly, and ordained both of them presbyters, with much force and compulsion. Then Peter remembered, and understood the foreknowledge and prophecy of the holy Zeno. Yet even after he had received the laying on of hands in this way, for seven years he refused to be counted among those in priestly ministry. He held out until he was found worthy even of the honour of the episcopate, in the time of the apostasy and transgression at Chalcedon. For it became known everywhere that all those apostate bishops had made their denial in writing. They had confirmed the wicked Tome of Leo and renewed the stale doctrines of Nestorius. Dioscorus, chief of the bishops of Egypt, a zealot for the truth and a fighter for the fear of God, had been cast into exile because he refused to submit to wickedness. Theodoret and Ibas, whose deposition had already been carried out by these very men, and who had been anathematized because their wickedness was plain, were received back without trial. And Flavian, who had been bishop of Constantinople and whose deposition had taken place for this very cause,

was restored by them after his death. Juvenal, the so-called high priest of Jerusalem, had surrendered to the transgression of the law and set his hand to it. He preferred the portion of Judas the betrayer, and returned with great pride. Yet before he went up to the synod he had loathed the so-called Tome of Leo and mocked the wickedness in it. He had testified to all the clergy and monks in Palestine: “It is Jewish, and the thinking in it is that of Simon the sorcerer, and whoever submits to it deserves to be circumcised.” The clergy and holy monks of Palestine had heard these words, and they were moved by divine zeal. First they went out on the road to meet this Juvenal, and earnestly begged him to remember his words, to loathe wickedness and to contend for the truth. When he was not persuaded, they gathered together in the holy city. They had our Lord Jesus Christ in their midst, he who had been denied by the wicked, helping his truth and his orthodox Church, which he redeemed with his blood. Inspired by his grace, and with zealous orthodox bishops among them, and the holy Romanus, father of monks, they chose the blessed Theodosius from the holy order. He was a man who had humbled himself from his youth in the practices of monasticism and was adorned with all the gifts of the fear of the Lord. He had already been through many contests, and at that very wicked synod he had shown his zeal for the orthodox faith. They set him up as high priest and shepherd of Jerusalem, the holy city. Having received the priesthood from God, he devoted all his diligence, care

and solicitude to keeping the apostolic faith pure in the churches under him. So he chose holy men from the order of holy monks and cross-bearers, men especially well attested in every evangelical way of life and in blameless faith. He ordained them bishops and confessors, and sent to each city the man suited to it, while the people of each city also cast their vote for the one chosen from among them. In this way they were received with all joy and gladness. When the patriarch performed an ordination, he testified in a loud voice to those being ordained: “I ordain you as martyrs and heralds of the orthodox faith.” For the times needed bishops like these. Then the inhabitants of Maiuma of Gaza were moved by divine power. They had known the blessed Peter for the long time he had lived among them, displaying every kind of excellence. At once the whole people ran to where he was living in quiet and seized him. He struggled hard against them, and grabbed the doors and bolted them when he saw them coming at him like raiders. Yet with great force, and with love, the people carried him off, lifted him up and put him on a litter. A crowd of prominent leaders and the clergy, with a great multitude around them [?], brought him to the holy city, so that the high priest might appoint him there as their shepherd and bishop. While they were travelling on the road and evening was already drawing near, they came to the village called Sokho.

The others lodged in the shops beside it. For the saint they arranged an upper room in the village to lodge in, with men able to guard him. In the middle of the night he was distressed by his thoughts and his heart was devouring him. As I said before, he always fled from honour, and he considered himself unworthy of the honour of the priesthood. He decided that he would rather die, if need be, than accept such a lot. In the dead of night, when everyone was weary from the toil of the journey and overcome by sleep, he asked his guards to let him go out onto the roof in front of the upper room, as if for a bodily need. They let him, and he went out alone. He was about to throw himself from the height onto the rocky ground below, expecting one of two things to happen: either he would somehow escape, or, being injured and no longer fit, he would be released from the compulsion of those leading him. As he was about to do this, a voice came to him saying: “Peter, Peter, if you do this, you will have no part with me.” So he was stopped from his attempt and was led to Jerusalem. There he protested violently, accused himself, and cried out many reasons by which he thought to show himself unworthy of the priesthood, and he bore witness against the one who was about to ordain him. But when divine grace had decreed it and he had received ordination, even then he refused to serve. He was shut up in a priestly residence, and at first he would not accept

the ministry, though everyone urged and begged him, the patriarch included. At last he was again threatened and commanded by a divine voice. So, when a synaxis was being held in the holy church of the place called Siloam, he came out running of his own accord, while everyone marvelled and was astonished. They assembled with the archbishop and the other bishops, all of whom went out to meet him with joy, gladness and amazement, praising God. Yet they were in great distress and bitterness, fearing that his refusal might become a cause of stumbling for many. He came to the holy church of Maiuma, escorted by all, and sat on the throne on the seventh of the month of Ab. It was a great, holy and heavenly feast, and life to the souls of all. The people were eager, and everyone longed to share in the saving mysteries from his holy hands. But again, out of great modesty, he hesitated to offer. He allowed the bishops and clergy to carry out the holy services, but at first he would not stand before the holy altar and complete the holy Eucharist. Finally the people grew angry and zealous, and supposed that it was true that he was thinking of flight. They ran at him, threatening to burn him and the church if he did not complete the synaxis for them. So, compelled in this way, he stood before the holy altar. Let whoever is watchful take heed of what follows. The greatness of God’s care, his love for mankind and his power must be proclaimed and made known boldly

everywhere, to encourage and strengthen the faithful and to establish the orthodox faith. We cannot keep silent about these things, for we heard them, and were convinced by the blessed one’s own words and by many who were near him at that time and celebrated with him. He did not yet know the holy prayers well, and had never read them before. Suddenly he was compelled to stand before the altar and complete the holy service, with great fear, dread and trembling. Some of the clergy stood by him who could prompt him if he skipped any of the required parts. When the time came, he made the invocation of the Holy Spirit and completed the whole anaphora. Then he came to the breaking of the holy bread, with all lamentation, contrition of heart and many tears, as was his custom. As he broke it, all of it began to flow with blood, so that the whole holy table was sprinkled. He was astonished, turned pale with trembling and drew back, and no longer dared to go on breaking the remaining loaves. As he was in this agitation, he turned and saw the Lord standing at his side, encouraging him and saying to him: “Bishop, break, do not fear. I have done this for the sake of my glory and not for yours, so that everyone may learn where the truth is, and who they are who hold the orthodox faith.” The miracle that took place then is repeated in everyone’s mouth to this day. He remained, then, in his holy church

for a period of about six months. Everyone was celebrating, rejoicing and calling the inhabitants of the city of Maiuma blessed for the excellence of God’s will and the appointment of such a high priest. They regarded him as an angel and hung on his love and affection. But the Accuser, who contends with God and envies, the first apostate, counsellor and patron of apostates, could not bear to see all this glory of God and the salvation of men. He feared a reversal, in which what had been diligently prepared in writing at Chalcedon against the fear of God would be undone. Through the emperor, who readily obeyed his commands, he brought about an imperial order. It decreed that the holy, true high priests, zealous for the fear of God, who had been appointed in all the cities of Palestine by Theodosius, the great and apostolic high priest, were to be driven from their thrones. If they refused, they were to be expelled by force and fall under sentence of death. And Theodosius, chief of the shepherds, was to suffer capital punishment wherever he was found, since the one whom the Accuser styled emperor had issued a decree against him. At that time all of them agreed and withdrew, for the patriarch Theodosius advised this, using words pleasing to God: that the heralds of the truth should be preserved, and that the orthodox peoples should not be bereaved by death and slaughter of those who built them up and supported

them. Then the blessed Peter moved to Egypt and, by the will of God, came to the city of Alexandria and hid there. In the days of Proterius the apostate he became a support and comfort to all the orthodox. No one who held the truth dared to show himself, neither cleric nor monk. But Peter, though in hiding, celebrated the divine services and gave provisions for life to all who asked, not letting their souls grow weak or their zeal and faith diminish. He was also found worthy to see a vision like this. A spectacle was being held in the city, at the place called the Theatre, and the whole people was gathered there. The believing people boiled with zeal, and suddenly, moved by divine power, they began to shout: “Dioscorus to the city! The orthodox one to the city! The confessor to his throne! Burn the bones of Proterius! Judas into exile! Throw Judas out!” They raised many other cries as well. They demanded that Dioscorus, the helper of godliness, return from his unjust exile and take his throne, and that the robber father and fighter against God, the new Caiaphas, be cast out and banished completely from the holy churches. But the rulers were eager to please in every way the man who held power at that time, and were looking after their own advantage.

They brought a multitude of armed soldiers and surrounded the Theatre. Threatening insult and slaughter, they terrified the people, so that as they fled outside, crushing one another in the narrow passages of the Theatre, many died. At that time the blessed Peter, still in hiding as I said, was celebrating the holy mysteries. In a state of ecstasy he saw many souls being escorted by angels and taken up to heaven.
