Then men came from the city and reported what had happened. The number of those who had died by violence in that crush and press was found to be the same as the number of souls the blessed one had counted while he was in that vision. Like the robber who was pronounced blessed, at that very moment these too bound on that same crown in a single hour through their confession of faith. For this is the reward kept for those who struggle and contend earnestly for the orthodox faith, even if they show their zeal only at the end of their lives. The blessed Peter could not stay hidden from the wicked Proterius, who was set on harming him even to the point of death, and sent murderous men by night to seize him and kill him. Yet Peter managed to escape, since our Lord, who saved and hid him, revealed the hidden plot to him. For when the men who had been sent came to the door of the place in the city where he was hiding and knocked,

pretending to be Orthodox and well-known people, they tried to persuade him: “This boy, they say, is in danger; let him be baptized before he dies.” But a holy voice said to him: “Do not open; they are lying in ambush.” Then he said to the brothers who were with him: “Let no one open the door. Whatever you see me do, do the same.” And when they had knelt in supplication and risen, he and the brothers with him cried out in a loud voice: “Our Father in heaven, help us against the robbers!” When the neighbours and those nearby heard and came running, the men lying in ambush fled. So, delivered from the snares of the hunters, as it is written, they left that place and moved to the upper regions of the Thebaid. And he came to the city of Oxyrhynchus, where there was a man named Moses, a man who loved Christ and loved the saints, and was clothed with excellence in faith and in purpose. The blessed one used to tell of him that, although he had an income of two thousand denarii a year, he would distribute half of it to the saints, the poor and strangers, and the other half went to his own needs and to the tax owed to the public treasury. Now this Oxyrhynchus is a great and priestly city of the Thebaid, in which the goodness of Christ so reigned that, since all its people were

Christians, there was a community of no fewer than ten thousand monks living in the monasteries around it. While he was there, it happened at that time that the wicked God-fighter Proterius devised and composed in writing, so they say, an anathema meant to lead the simple astray. In it he crafted, and craftily set down, the wickedness of the synod of Chalcedon, with much evil artifice and hypocrisy, mixing poison with honey. When this was read before all the people and he could not shake anyone from these foundations, he sent a copy of it to the bishops under him who had agreed to submit to his rebellion, commanding that it be read before all the people of every city. So when the bishop of Oxyrhynchus received it and read it before all the people, with the devil's help he was shameless enough to mislead many of the Orthodox and shake them. And since many were in danger of stumbling, simple as they were and untrained in such artifice and hypocrisy, the blessed Peter was urged by the leading men of the city, by his host, who was a zealous man, and by the holy monks to read it, to expose the deceit and the plot, and openly to proclaim the truth before all the people. After being asked many times, being untrained in such tumults and in speaking boldly before the people, he was at last constrained and gave himself up

to bear witness. So they took him and set him in the public square, in a high place, on the base of a column on which the emperor's statue stood. Holding in his hands that paper of the snare, he was pondering anxiously how to expose the deceit hidden in it. And suddenly he saw the blessed Theodosius, bishop of Jerusalem, that new James, who had ordained him and who had already been perfected in confession and martyrdom in the royal city in the days of the God-hating emperor Marcian. (We shall tell the manner of his death later, God willing.) He saw him standing at his right hand, pointing with his finger, showing and exposing the wickedness hidden in every word. What he heard from him he spoke to the people, our Lord being near and helping him and granting him boldness together with grace. And having in this way persuaded the people and confirmed them all, being seen and praised by all as an angel, he snatched them from the nets of error. At that time the blessed Dioscorus, chief of bishops, having put to shame the loathsome [?] dragon and his ministers and favourites, fought the noble contest of confession, finished his course, and kept the apostolic faith unbroken to the end, and was perfected while in exile in the city of Gangra, the metropolis of Paphlagonia,

having been bishop seven years and three months. The day on which he fell asleep was the seventh of Elul. When the bitter and painful news of him reached the city of the Alexandrians, the crowds of the Orthodox people, the holy monks and the nuns were broken in spirit by severe suffering and distress, for they now gave up hope of their deliverance. But that harsh father, the bloodthirsty Proterius, exulted and boasted with great joy and delight, as one who now held a secure leadership free of disturbance. From then on he inflicted harsh evils on the laity and the monks who would not enter into communion with him. He bribed the magistrates, and through their hands brought every kind of unbearable affliction and distress upon the Orthodox, bringing into the city bands of wild and barbarous soldiers. He filled it with untold evils and great lamentation, and committed lawless and unnatural acts without mercy, so that he even stretched out his madness against holy virgins. But the just, mighty and long-suffering Judge, who strikes and heals, chastises and restores, would not bear any longer with such evils. The Lord awoke as one asleep, made his spear flash, and with it slew the crooked dragon, I mean Marcian, the new Assyrian: an angel struck him on the neck with an incurable wound, as if with a sword, so that those who saw it with their own eyes and were convinced bore witness to it. Then

the blessed Peter left Oxyrhynchus and turned towards Alexandria. It was God who turned him back there, for the sake of a divine dispensation that was about to come to pass, for the consolation of the faithful people and for the restoration and establishment of the orthodox faith. It was this. When the news of the death of Marcian, the head, cause and mainstay of such evils, reached the city of the Alexandrians, those faithful peoples who had long been tormented and distressed by the many oppressions and persecutions that had come upon them, as has been said, and whose hands had grown weak, found a time of respite and came to life again. They offered thanksgiving, acknowledging his goodness, and gave praise to Christ the Saviour, who had not been angry to the end and delivered them into the hands of that destructive, bloodthirsty father. Seeing a time that suited them and was dear to them, the crowds of holy monks gathered: not only those in the city itself, but also those near it, at the place called the Enaton, at the Oktokaidekaton and the Eikoston, and the rest of the holy monasteries, together with all the faithful and zealous people of the city of Alexandria. They had their own head and leader, and to this end

he roused them and stirred them up according to the will of God: the blessed humble man and great prophet Longinus, father of monks. When they had all taken counsel together, he sent men suited to the task. Without his having learned of it beforehand or suspected anything, they snatched from the desert the holy Timothy, that excellent confessor and true martyr, who long before had been honoured with the dignity of the priesthood by the great Cyril, chief of bishops, together with his brother Anatolius, who was fervent and his equal in zeal. He was a man adorned with every apostolic way of life and virtue, and above all with fervour and warm zeal for the orthodox faith. They brought him to the city, to the church called the Caesarion, where the whole city had gathered as one, so to speak, with women and children and the holy monks, and they hastened to ordain him and make him high priest, herald and champion of piety. But only one of the Orthodox bishops could be found, Eusebius of Pelusium, because the others were persecuted and in hiding and did not dare to show themselves. Then it became known to the people, by the will of God, that our blessed Peter was there in hiding, and the people ran and came suddenly to the place where the blessed one was living.

They took him by force, lifted him on their shoulders and carried him to the Caesarion, where the crowds of the people were, who were urging that this be done in accordance with the ancient laws and customs for times of persecution. The blessed one had already been informed by God that this was his will, just as he many times secretly revealed things to his dear friends; and so it was with this bishop Timothy, for the goodness of God was near at that time and was bringing everything about. But while all were overwhelmed by the joy and gladness of such a hope, the blessed Peter managed to slip away, passing through the crowd and going off to hide. The Lord who had revealed it to him concealed him, for he feared he might do something like Philip the apostle, who, when he had baptized the believer of Candace, was immediately seen no more. For the blessed one always fled from the honour and glory of men, as something that hindered the stillness he loved, which nothing must take from him, and his undisturbed converse with God; yet he was never allowed, right to the end, to reach his goal as he desired. For when the ordination of the great high priest Timothy had thus

been completed, in the beauty of God's will, by the choice, desire and vote of the people of the Alexandrians and of the holy, cross-bearing monks, unspeakable joy and exultation took hold of the souls of all, and the peoples rejoiced and were glad. But that wicked and in every way unclean Proterius, seeing himself in danger, grew all the more furious. With much gold he bribed the magistrates, above all the one called the stratelates, whose name was Dionysius, a murderous man fierce in anger, and stirred him to such madness that, with a multitude of armed soldiers, wild and barbarous, he rushed upon God's holy church, killed without mercy many of the laity, monks and nuns, wounded many others with blows and left them half dead. And at last he did not shrink from forcing his way into the baptistery and, from the holy Jordan, that is, from the font of the adorable baptism, violently seizing the holy Timothy with his brother Anatolius. They carried him off to Taposiris, a desert fort thirty miles from the city, and imprisoned him there under guard of soldiers, so that from then on the wicked Proterius, having found an opportunity suited to his madness, might once again inflict many evils on the monks and laity who would not share in his wickedness, and above all on

those who had desired the ordination of the blessed Timothy. Unable to bear it, they gave up hope; their souls were now full and sated with distress, and they were inflamed with a martyr's zeal. Day after day they drew up for battle against the soldiers and stirred up a civil war, with killing and bloodshed. So the leading men of the city and the one called the stratelates feared that such a great city of the emperor might be destroyed, since he had not yet learned, nor had it been reported to him, what had happened, and he would be enraged with them; for already news had spread everywhere of the good order and benevolence of the new emperor Leo. They resolved together to take Proterius too out of the city, carry him off to some place and keep him under guard, until they could inform the emperor and he could give whatever order he pleased concerning each of them. But as Proterius was being led out by the soldiers, one of them was seized with zeal and killed him, on the fourth of Nisan, twenty days after the ordination of the blessed Timothy; he had sat on the throne five years and six months. When this happened, the laity and the soldiers all fled together, and he was left thrown in the market place like a pig or a dog, whom he had resembled in his conduct and his faithlessness, having plucked destruction for himself. As for the events that took place in this affair, which have come to the ears of all

the God-fearing, we leave it to others to relate and write them down. For even if the one who suffered deserved it, it is not fitting for us either to hear or to tell such things. Nevertheless we see, as it is written, that the divine word was fulfilled upon him: “Evils will hunt the unjust man to destruction”; and, “You have humbled the proud like the slain”; and, “The Lord sets himself against the proud”; and, “The wicked is kept for the day of his ruin.” When news of these things was sent to the emperor Leo, he took pity on the afflictions that had befallen the city of the Alexandrians all this time. And sparing those who had been carried away [?], he commanded that the blessed Timothy, who had received the laying on of hands from God, should return and take his throne; and so the city would be at peace, the people would find relief, and they would gain consolation for the evils that had passed. And this indeed came about for them through the return of the blessed Timothy: everywhere one could see the joy, gladness and exultation that filled the city, as many crowds of unbelievers ran to be baptized. In short, the city of the Alexandrians was heaven in those days. But when the blessed Timothy had remained in the episcopate for seven years, the envious demon, who cannot bear to see the salvation of men, again stirred up to anger and to wicked and envious zeal the bishops

everywhere, and above all the one in Constantinople and the one in Rome. For the good order, the glory, the way of life and the boldness of the blessed one were a shame and reproach to them, since every day the wicked synod of Chalcedon was openly anathematized by him and by the bishops under him, by clergy, monks and laity. They exerted themselves on every side with great haste, with gifts and with the patronage of wicked men, and since they found that those in power at the time were won over by the love of money, they did not cease from their malice and wickedness until, with much killing of the people and shedding of blood, they had the blessed Timothy exiled to the city of Gangra, where the victorious crown-bearer of confession, the high priest Dioscorus, his fellow confessor, had been perfected. This was why the blessed Peter could not, as he prayed and desired, withdraw from among men and delight in the stillness he loved. For when Timothy, chief of bishops, had gone out and been handed over to exile by royal command and authority, another of the presbyters entered in his place by royal command. His name was Timothy, but he was more often called Salophaciolus, and under that guise he held to the wicked doctrine of the Chalcedonians. When Peter, that delight of God and son of the zeal

of the great Moses, saw the oppression of the faithful brothers, who had been left bereft and deprived of those who edified and supported them, and were in danger of being shaken from the truth of the faith, he took up divine zeal, pressing himself even unto death, as he pondered and meditated in everything those blessed words of the apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” And leaving the stillness he loved, as though there were no time for it, he went again to the city of the Alexandrians and to the holy monasteries around it, and to many other cities and villages of Egypt, going about everywhere in secret. He built up and supported the communities of the Orthodox, and became another Paul the apostle, all things to all men. By word and deed, by his way of life and conduct, he gave a model for teaching the ways of piety and divine zeal. What wonders and great signs he performed there through divine grace and the power that attended him, and how many healings and mighty works, it is beyond our weakness to write them all. But we shall recall one or two, and leave the rest to those who learned of them by experience and by sight, to tell and relate. The daughter of one of the notables of the city was ill with a grievous sickness. She was his only daughter, and he loved her as an only child. Her mother was a lover of Christ

and a believer, and she took great delight in the saints. The father, though a Christian, was much in the grip of the error and love of the pagan philosophers. So when a certain chief of the sorcerers promised him that he would heal the girl if he took her by night to the Serapeum and there performed upon her the rites and defilements of the arts of sorcery, he readily listened and was ready to hand the girl over. When her mother learned this from a servant who had noticed it, who was a Christian and a great believer, she at once sent to the blessed Peter, informing him of the devil's plot and imploring him not to neglect her, her husband and the girl, who were in danger of falling into true death by provoking the Lord. When the blessed one heard this, he was inflamed with zeal and cried out in a loud voice: “Lord, let that wicked man not live!” Having said this, he at once took some of the saints who were with him and went by night to the girl's mother. He found her sitting beside her daughter, tearing herself with weeping and lamentation, and also keeping watch that the girl should not be handed over by her husband to that wicked man. He ordered all the others to go out, took oil and anointed the girl. Then he gave her the holy mysteries, comforted her mother with many words of comfort, and urged her to trust without doubting in Christ, the Lord of life;

and he went back to where he was staying. The next day the girl was found healed and freed from that grievous sickness, while the philosopher who fought against God was buried dead. The saint's sentence had swiftly decreed that he should come to his end in this way, when in his anger he cried out: “Lord, let that wicked man not live!” So the wonder became known throughout the whole city, and everyone praised God for the grace given to his saints; they ran to the blessed one and clung to him, and were strengthened all the more in the orthodox faith. For this sign also took place at that time. He was going by night with those who attended him to the house of a rich man to visit a sick person, and was passing a place where there stood a very large statue of Julian the apostate, when the demon produced an apparition: the statue came down from where it stood and ran after them. When those walking with him perceived the commotion and disturbance and saw the apparition, they were terrified and cried out, calling on the blessed one to help them. He made as if he had noticed nothing, though he knew well, and went on his way without turning back. But as they were afraid and clutching at his garments, the blessed one turned, called on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and breathed on the apparition,

and at once it dissolved like smoke and was seen no more. The blessed one also used to tell of this, which happened in those days in Alexandria. One of the lovers of Christ persuaded some of the saints to come to his house, bless him and share his table, for those Alexandrians are very eager and diligent in this matter. The man was one of the eminent notables. He also persuaded them, he said, to bring me along with them. Those fathers knew my poverty, which finds such invitations difficult because of great weakness; yet they pressed me hard, saying that since the man was zealous and eager, it was not right to offend him. When we came, we reclined at table. And as we were eating, he began to give orders to the servants who were waiting on us, and to scold them with unseemly words that come from the evil habits of the world, as if he had forgotten with whom he was reclining and eating. While he persisted in these shameful words, a voice came to me saying: “Peter, Peter, my name is being blasphemed, and you sit and take your ease!” No one heard the voice speak but I alone. Troubled and weeping, I waited to understand clearly. When the voice came a third time, and I could not hold back my tears, I withdrew from among the others as if I were in a hurry because of some need, and so I went out and hurried to my cell, sighing all the way

and mourning. And I reflected how nothing escapes God's notice, not even the things that seem small to an eye that is not pure, neither deed nor word. And this indeed is what the wise Solomon said: “The spirit of the Lord fills the whole world, and he who holds all things together has knowledge of every voice; therefore no one who speaks iniquity is hidden, nor does he escape the judgement of reproof; and the report of his words comes to the Lord, to reprove his wickedness, for the ear of zeal hears all things.” And our Lord said in the Gospel: “For every idle word, account will be given on the day of judgement.” Yet the blessed one used to say that this became the occasion of salvation and of a change for the better for the man who had invited them. For the Lord does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live. And another fearful and awe-inspiring story compels me not to leave it out, which the blessed one also told as having happened at that time. “When I was about to offer the oblation,” he said, “outside the city in one of the holy monasteries, some of the lovers of Christ came before the liturgy. They were telling of something that had happened in the city, which held no edification or profit for those who heard it. I kept silent, not accepting what was being said,

but neither did I stop them, because I did not want to shame them, for they were among the illustrious men of the city. But having let it pass in silence, I went in to offer the oblation. And when I stood before the holy altar, I saw an angel, fearful and awe-inspiring in appearance, who came in anger, seized me by the waist and wanted to throw me down from the bema. As I wept and wailed and asked what the reason was, he said: ‘Why, when you were about to enter into the service of God and stand before the holy altar, did you let yourself be drawn into such talk?’ And when I said, ‘You know, Lord, that I did not agree with it even in appearance, nor did any of what was said so much as enter my heart,’ he said: ‘Then why did you let yourself even hear such idle words?’ None of those who were nearby heard this, nor saw the vision of the angel, but I alone. Yet they saw that I was trembling and in anguish, and overcome with distress. At last the angel said: ‘See, this is forgiven you this once. Take care from now on, when you are about to stand before the altar and celebrate the mysteries, that you stand clear and pure, keeping yourself from all idle talk and empty words.’ And having said this, the angel was no longer seen.” This the blessed one carefully observed to his last breath. All these things, and others like them and greater still, when

they became known to the fathers in Palestine and to the brothers and the Orthodox peoples, stirred and kindled them all to love for their holy father and bishop. And many saints came to him from Palestine, for his flock was the Lord's; and let it not be unknown that all this time it was guided by his oversight and spiritual teaching. So when he had spent no small time in Alexandria and the rest of Egypt, and had sufficiently built them up and strengthened them, he was at last persuaded, as I have said, or rather commanded by God, without whom he did nothing, and turned to the regions of Palestine. He came to the city of Ascalon, where he was gladly received by the fathers and brothers there, and settled in a village called Peleia [?], about ten stadia from the city. While he lived there, many came to him from everywhere: some he strengthened; others he enlightened and added to the orthodox church; and some, whom he had thoroughly prepared to renounce the vanity of the world, he persuaded to press on towards perfection, to distribute their possessions to the poor, and, taking up the cross of Christ, to cling to him alone. Among them were the blessed Procopius, who renounced everything and was formed into a true man of God, and Cyril, that pledge

of Christ. Both of these he brought out of the world and led to the place of the angels. There was also Theodore, who had been a scholasticus, who later became heir to his evangelical way of life, his zeal and the leadership of his monastery, together with Abba John, the honoured old man, beloved and dear, adorned with every excellence of the monastic life and above all with humility.
